newsitem.title: UK: Dlr seen sustaining solid tone in data-packed week.
newsitem.headline: Dlr seen sustaining solid tone in data-packed week.

text.p: The dollar looks set to maintain its firm tone, underpinned by expectations that a slate of U.S. economic data due for release this week will keep interest rate rise speculation on the boil, analysts said.

A rise of 262,000 in U.S. non-farm payrolls in December, released last Friday, helped fire interest rate rise fever, even more so as an increase in average hourly earnings of 0.5 percent set inflation alarm bells ringing.
Widening U.S.-German yield spreads and its resilience to credit market gyrations buoy the U.S. unit, analysts said.
"Dollar/mark should continue to benefit from the increasing interest rate spread between the U.S. and Germany," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN Amro in London.

The dollar remained close to 29-month highs against the mark at 1.5861 marks at 1205 GMT after peaking at 1.5873 on Friday following the release of the U.S. jobs report. It closed at 1.5852/57 in Europe on Friday.
Against the yen it traded at 116.46/51, up from 115.96/116.01 but below its 45-month high at 117 yen hit on January 6.
Norfield said a strong dollar signal was coming from the yield differential between 10-year bonds in real terms.

The 10-year yield spread between the U.S. and Germany has widened to 84 from 60 in December, he said. "The widening yield spread gives higher returns against Germany, leaving the dollar with pretty decent support."

The December jobs report led many economists to revise their forecasts on the strength of the economy. Some see a growing risk of a rise in U.S. rates at the next meeting of the policy-making Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) on February 4-5.
December consumer price data, due on Tuesday, will be closely watched for further signs of inflationary pressure, traders said.

The risk of a dollar setback from U.S. data, in particular if CPI figures were stronger-than-expected, looked less threatening after the currency's resilient performance in the wake of the payrolls' release, traders said.

The benchmark 30-year Treasury bond fell nearly two points on Friday to 6.90 percent before recovering back to 6.85 percent. But the dollar shrugged off bond market fears, broke key resistance at 1.5840 marks and set a fresh two-year high.
"The dollar will now head for 1.60. There is stil good demand for dollars, especially as the mark is weak across the board," said Nick Shamin, currency analyst at Technical Data.
Dollar-positive interest rate expectations were highlighted last week by another rise in German unemployment in December and a downbeat outlook for fourth-quarter 1996 growth in Germany.

U.S. November trade data, due for release on Friday, could be a thorn in the dollar's side though and will be scrutinised for signs of a widening gap with Japan. The overall deficit is seen rising to $9.8 billion from $7.99 billion the previous month.
Even though rate rise speculation has increased, market watchers caution that the optimism might be premature.
"I don't see a rate rise at the next FOMC meeting," said Pat Magill, head of the corporate desk at Daiwa Europe.
Dollar/yen has been volatile lately amid rumours of Japanese capital repatriation as a result of sharp losses in Japan's stockmarket. However, so far there is little evidence of that.

"We still see an upside bias on dollar/yen," sad ABN Amro's Norfield. "This view is based on capital outflows out of Japan by investors looking for higher yield and the shaky financial prospects of investing in Japan."
Japanese officials dished out plenty of verbal intervention last week to stem the yen's decline.
"Dollar/yen might find it a bit harder to go up beyond 117 yen but there there is good demand on dips towards 115.80," said Magill at Daiwa.
